FeRx fits nonlinear mixed-effects models defined in a small, readable DSL
(`.ferx` files), powered by a Rust engine. There are two ways to run it:

- **From R** — the `ferx-r` package wraps the engine, takes a `data.frame`, and
  returns a fit object you can plot and report on.
- **From the command line** — the `ferx` CLI reads a `.ferx` model plus a CSV
  and writes results to disk. No R involved.

Both call the same engine and produce the **same estimates**. If you'd rather
not install Rust at all, both also come prebuilt in a
[Docker image](#run-with-docker).

---

## Run from R

### Prerequisites

The R package compiles the Rust engine from source, so a **stable Rust
toolchain** and **cmake** must be present *before* you install it. `pak` does
not install them for you — without them the install fails at the compile step.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## macOS

```bash
brew install cmake
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh
source "$HOME/.cargo/env"
```

## Linux

```bash
sudo apt install cmake            # Debian/Ubuntu; use your package manager
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh
source "$HOME/.cargo/env"
```

## Windows

Install [Rtools45](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/) (it bundles
cmake) and [rustup](https://www.rust-lang.org/tools/install), then add the
GNU-ABI toolchain in PowerShell:

```powershell
rustup toolchain install stable-x86_64-pc-windows-gnu
```

The package build pins this toolchain automatically — no `rustup default`
needed.

:::

Verify the toolchain is visible before continuing:

```bash
rustc --version
cmake --version
```

The first install compiles the Rust backend: roughly 15-30 minutes on a fast
machine, up to 1-2 hours on an older laptop. Later installs reuse Cargo's cache
and are much faster.

Platform gotchas — notably RStudio on macOS starting with a PATH that hides
`cargo` — are covered in the
**[installation chapter](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-book/chapters/01-installation.html)**
of the ferx-r book.

### Install

```r
pak::pak("FeRx-NLME/ferx-r")
```

Then fit the bundled warfarin example:

```r
library(ferx)
ex  <- ferx_example("warfarin")
fit <- ferx_fit(ex$model, ex$data)
print(fit)
```

`ferx_example()` (no argument) lists all bundled examples.

To skip the Rust build, see [Run with Docker](#run-with-docker). For platform
notes and the full R workflow — diagnostics, simulation, covariates, IOV —
see the **[ferx-r book](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-book/)**.

---

## Run from the CLI

The CLI ships with `ferx-core`. Building it from source needs the same stable
Rust toolchain as above (`cargo build --release`). Point it at a `.ferx` model
and a CSV:

```bash
ferx warfarin.ferx --data warfarin.csv
```

It writes the fit results (estimates, predictions) to disk next to the inputs.

For building the CLI, estimation settings, the `.ferx` DSL spec, and using the
engine as a Rust library, see the **[ferx-core book](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-core/)**.

---

## Run with Docker

A prebuilt image with R, the ferx package and the `ferx` CLI — no Rust
toolchain, no compile step — is published for `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`:

```bash
docker pull ghcr.io/ferx-nlme/ferx-r:latest
```

Mount your project at `/work` and run an R script or the CLI there:

```bash
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" ghcr.io/ferx-nlme/ferx-r:latest Rscript fit.R
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" ghcr.io/ferx-nlme/ferx-r:latest \
  ferx model.ferx --data data.csv
```

`:latest` tracks the development branch. The `:release` tag and fixed version
tags (e.g. `:0.5.0`) arrive with the next release; validated work should pin a
version tag and record its digest rather than use `:latest`.

For tags, pinning by digest, thread settings and the RStudio Server image, see
the **[installation chapter](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-book/chapters/01-installation.html#sec-docker)**
of the ferx-r book.
